title: Stroke Lab
user: Digital artists and maintainers of browser/cross-platform drawing tools who need to isolate whether a bad stroke comes from smoothing, device sampling, rendering, or undo history.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Pixel-art users compare several editors and report cursor behavior and platform reliability concerns, showing that feel and basic input quality determine tool choice.
A pen-tablet user asks to disable auto-smoothing because delayed strokes and dotted i's break handwriting flow, despite other apps working without delay.

recurrence: Artist feedback spans pixel editors and web whiteboards; even small latency destroys trust because drawing is continuous motor feedback.
current_workaround: Switch apps, toggle an undocumented smoothing setting, screen-record a bad stroke, or submit an issue without timing evidence.
incumbents_and_gap: Browser devtools profile frames and professional tablet diagnostics, but neither provides a creator-readable trace of pointer sample rate, coalescing, smoothing delay, raster delay, and undo cost.
smallest_useful_product: A local web test pad plus embeddable JS probe that records anonymized pointer timing, draws raw versus smoothed traces, and exports a reproducible issue bundle. Non-goals: replacing brush engines, driver installation, or cloud telemetry.
success_measure: A maintainer can classify a supplied bad-stroke report as input, smoothing, render, or history-related in under ten minutes in 80% of pilot cases.
monetization: free — broad integration and transparent diagnostics matter more than gating a frustrating input problem; paid support is possible.
constraints: Never capture drawing content by default; support pen pressure/tilt only with explicit consent; disclose browser timestamp precision limits.
why_distinct: It measures and explains drawing feel; it is not a new canvas editor or a thin AI brush wrapper.
